title: How to Not Kill Yourself
subtitle: A handy guide, as the 1000th post on The Frontier Psychiatrists Newsletter.
body_html:
This is the 1000th article on The Frontier Psychiatrists newsletter. Better make it good, right? Much of the advice around suicide prevention is maddeningly vague. If there's something we don't need, as it relates to suicide, it's vagaries.

"Get help.”

“Reach out.”

“Address Risk Factors”

It goes on in that format. A lot of the advice from people around suicide prevention is informed by little personal experience. If you wanna learn how to knit, it would be strange to ask someone who has never knit before. You wouldn't expect them to have meaningful guidance.

This article is intended to be guidance for people who are at risk of suicide. Yes, it's for you— directly, and specifically. It's not just gonna be about crisis, and what to do in moments of it. I'm writing a guide to help my co-travelers do their very best to reduce the risk that they're ever gonna die by suicide.

And he to me: “This miserable mode
Maintain the melancholy souls of those
Who lived withouten infamy or praise.”

—Dante’s Inferno, Canto III, Longfellow Translation

I should probably have some credentials for this endeavor? I'm a psychiatrist, for both kids, adolescents, and adults, and perhaps more importantly, a person with bipolar disorder who has had suicidal thoughts on and off throughout my life. Sometimes they've been bad. Professionally, I've worked with people who are suicidal, specifically, on purpose, and most of them have lived. I don't know, that's because I'm very special—most people with suicidal ideation will survive. But I faced the darkness, and I'm here to tell the tale, and to bring you back something that I strive to be practical. I've had a challenging weekend, and I lost someone I really cared about, as I wrote just this week. For my readers, who might be worried, I'm doing OK, if very sad.

The audience for this article is the people who realize they're at risk for suicide, and would like not to have their lives end that way. I hope it's useful to others, such as those who are wondering what they can do to help, who I suspect to be a rather large cohort. Policy makers might read it, and I wouldn't dissuade them, but this is an article for those who want, desperately, to live, while knowing all too well the siren’s song.

Suicide: It’s Often Impulsive

One of the most important things to understand about death by suicide is that much of it happens impulsively:

Attempts were considered impulsive if the respondent reported spending less than 5 minutes between the decision to attempt suicide and the actual attempt. Among the 153 case-subjects, 24% attempted impulsively…

When talking about risk for suicide, we end up falling back on risk factors, as much of our understanding is built on retrospective analysis, which is all well and good, but you're trying to live prospectively, and not die in the future! One takeaway about impulsive suicide is that it's not all about depression:

Relative to control subjects, male sex, fighting, and hopelessness distinguished impulsive cases but depression did not.1

Recommendation One: Live As Your Authentic Self

If you're not living as your authentic self, the time to do so is as soon as you can, subject to physical and psychological safety. It's hard to hold onto living when you hate doing the living you're doing. If there's something about your life that you absolutely hate, that you feel trapped in, and you feel like it's going to kill you, it might. Change it. Going back-and-forth about whether you should live authentically to who you are? It's not worth it. Living as someone you're not just to keep other people off your back is a solvable problem—get different people, who don't wanna be on your back for who you are. Get the fuck out, live authentically.

This recommendation is easier said than done, but I wanted to get it out of the way early, in case the people who needed to hear it subsequently wander off and don't read the rest.

When it comes to gender dysphoria, specifically:

A supportive environment for social transition and timely access to gender reassignment, for those who required it, emerged as key protective factors.2

It’s hard to argue against the supportive social environment for anybody, no matter what they're feeling. However, for those who feel profoundly out of place, a supportive social environment can be life-saving. Although this article is aimed at those who might be thinking about suicide, for the rest of us, I will highlight that being that supportive social environment might save lives that you care about, whether you know it in advance or not.

Being loving and supportive, generally, is life-saving—it's primary prevention for despair among those you care about most, before you even know there's a problem.

Recommendation Two: Don’t Keep Secrets

Keeping your problems a secret is a terrible idea. It’s also laden:

the authors review the theories and empirical findings concerning the consequences of revealing personal secrets (i.e., ones that directly involve the secret keeper). Most of the literature has suggested that revealing personal secrets is advantageous to the secret keeper. However, choosing to reveal secrets is a complex decision that can have disturbing consequences, such as being rejected by and alienated from the listener. Such rejection may lead the revealer to construct a negative self-image.3

It’s risky to reveal them, and all the more so for those who feel they have much to lose (Kelly, 1999):

On the other hand, secret keepers can avoid looking bad before important audiences (such as their bosses or therapists) by not revealing their secrets.

It makes sense to have a confidant:

Making a wise decision to reveal a personal secret hinges on finding an appropriate confidant—someone who is discreet, who is perceived by the secret keeper to be nonjudgmental, and who is able to offer new insights into the secret.4

Secrets can feel really big, scary, and devastating, because we don't have a way to check them against any kind of yardstick. How big a secret is, emotionally, can't be measured, because somebody else's perspective is the ruler that gives us the sense of scale. If you've ever had a conversation with somebody about a hard time, and had them respond, "You think that's bad, let me tell you about X!” you'll get a sense of how human it is, and how much a relief it is, to have an understanding of scale. Either go find out your secret is really bad, and you'll feel validated that you've been carrying around something really heavy, which makes it less heavy. Or, on the other hand, it won't seem so bad after all. What you need to make this trick work is, of course, a confidant. A therapist is pretty good in this role, and if you don't have other confidants in your life, or even if you do, it's a great idea to have a therapist.

Infected minds
To their deaf pillows will discharge their secrets.
More needs she the divine than the physician.
God, God forgive us all. Look after her.
Remove from her the means of all annoyance
And still keep eyes upon her. So, good night.
My mind she has mated, and amazed my sight.
I think but dare not speak.

—The Doctor, Macbeth, Act 5 Scene 1

Recommendation Three: See A Therapist Who’s Not Scared Off By Suicidal Ideation

We have some really good psychotherapies to reduce the risk of suicide. For those treatments to work, you have to get one of them for yourself. That means you have to take the risk of seeing a therapist. It means with that therapist, you'd have to tell them about what you're thinking—including suicidal thoughts. All of that is kind of a big ask for many of us—especially helpers ourselves. It can be embarrassing, humiliating, shameful, and generate fear that you're gonna be involuntarily hospitalized, which I've already addressed many times in this newsletter. Still, it isn't particularly helpful in preventing suicide and may be harmful.

Some therapies, particularly in the outpatient setting, are proven to be helpful. Most of these have been proven to be helpful in populations that had a high rate of suicide attempts, so that we could tell the difference.

The most used psychotherapeutic treatments were dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT, 27.5%) and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT, 15.0%) in patients with a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder (32.5%) and depression (15.0%). Despite the between-study heterogeneity, interventions lead to a reduction in suicidal outcomes, i.e., suicidal ideation (55.0%) and suicide attempts (37.5%).5

Effective psychotherapy can also improve your symptoms over time, even years after the treatment has concluded. This was highlighted in this now-classic study about mentalization-based treatment with eight-year follow-up:

Five years after discharge from mentalization-based treatment, [the treatment] group continued to show clinical and statistical superiority to treatment as usual on suicidality (23% versus 74%).6

I doubt it matters tremendously, which modality you choose, but it does matter that you like your therapist, and that you feel safe, talking about suicidal thoughts with them, if you want to be helpful with your suicidal thoughts.

However, a good sign that a therapist will be a good fit for someone who is thinking about suicidality is just to discuss this with them. Find out how they think about the problem, and especially if they advertise working with suicidal people, or training in DBT, MBT, TFP, Schema Therapy, or the like, you won't be the first suicidal patient they've seen. You're unlikely to be the last.

The other benefit of this, from a practical standpoint, is that if you're having a really challenging day, and you have to talk to someone in your life about it, and they freak out, you can reassure that person by letting them know you're talking to your therapist about it. There's a tendency to chill out and assume that somebody has a handle on the problem, even if your jumpy, uncomfortable friend doesn't feel that way personally. Having a therapist is both practical and helpful.

Recommendation Three: Don’t Drink

Alcohol makes it endlessly more likely that you're gonna die by suicide. OK, that's hyperbole; it's not endlessly more likely; it's measurably and empirically more likely:

Prevalence estimates of alcohol abuse among completed suicides were mainly obtained in psychological autopsy studies and were reported in 8 reviews. The estimates varied between 15 and 61%.

And the authors further highlighted:

Prevalence of alcohol intoxication in completed suicide was covered by 3 reviews including altogether 35 adult population studies … prevalence rates ranged between 6 and 69 %.

Prevalence of alcohol intoxication in attempted suicide …was described in one review of 15 primary studies … and prevalence rates ranged between 10 and 73 %.

And certainly consider not being an alcoholic, or getting treatment for your alcohol use disorder, or maybe even just being a little bit quicker to get the GLP-1, as I wrote the other day:

Life time risk of suicide in alcohol abusers (i.e. alcoholics) was reviewed in one study (Murphy and Wetzel 1990) … ranging between 1.8 % and 6.2 %.7

Recommendation Four: Don’t Use Coke or Other Drugs.

Similar to alcohol use disorder, cocaine use puts humans at higher rates of death by suicide, and if you're gonna abstain from any drug, if you're worried about suicide, it should be cocaine.

However, there are some individuals for whom this is particularly true. In that spirit of fully informed advice, I'm gonna highlight the individuals who are most likely to have a suicide attempt related to their cocaine use, because it's not equally risky for everybody.

Do you have childhood trauma? Then cocaine makes suicide attempts more likely:

The cocaine-dependent patients who had attempted suicide had significantly higher childhood trauma scores for emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional neglect, and physical neglect than the cocaine-dependent patients who had never attempted suicide…

And a family history of suicide makes cocaine a riskier choice:

Twenty-one of the 84 patients who had attempted suicide (25.0%) had a family history of suicidal behavior, compared with seven of the 130 patients who had never attempted suicide (5.4%) (χ2=15.58, df=1, p<0.0001; odds ratio=5.88, 95% CI=2.38–14.44).

It's not like people are doing thorough risk assessments before deciding to blow a line, but if you're unlike me and cool enough to be at parties where people might offer you cocaine, and you know that there's a risk of this, given your family history or personal history, you can now take that into account.

Unfortunately, other “fun” drugs of abuse are not known to be particularly safer, specifically opioids and cannabis:

Furthermore, one study found that opiates were present in 20% of suicide deaths, marijuana in 10.2%, cocaine in 4.6%, and amphetamines in 3.4% (2). Among the reported substances, alcohol and opioids are associated with the greatest risks of suicidal behavior.8

Recommendation Five: Treat Your Psychiatric Illness, if You Have One

Psychiatric disorders, in Western cultures, are highly correlated with death by suicide. They're also highly prevalent, so it's not the most useful statistic in the world. That hasn't been said, there's some specific psychiatric disorders that are more likely to lead to your death than others, and if you know you have one of these, getting treatment is a priority if you either want to live, or really want to not die by suicide. I know those two things are not necessarily always the same, which is why I said it that way:

Ninety percent of people who die by suicide have one or more concomitant psychiatric disorders (3). Suicide risk is highest among patients with bipolar disorder (odds ratio=7.77) and unipolar affective disorder (odds ratio=6.67), followed by schizophrenia (odds ratio=6.55) and anxiety disorders (odds ratio=3.57–6.64).9

If you have bipolar disorder, the answer is relatively easy, at least when it comes to the data, which is to give lithium a try. I've written about this extensively, but lithium-treated patients with bipolar disorder—who are axiomatically bipolar patients who can tolerate lithium—have an up to 800% reduction in the risk of death by suicide.

It works better if you take it, by the way:

The observed rates of suicide were 0.143, and of attempts, 2.01%/year, with a 5.2-fold (95% CI: 1.5–18.6) greater risk among patients consistently rated poorly versus highly adherent to lithium prophylaxis (11.4/2.2 acts/100 person-years).

Similarly, with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, we have great data on clozapine in preventing suicide, even compared to an active treatment like olanzapine:

Suicidal behavior was significantly less in patients treated with clozapine vs olanzapine (hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% confidence interval, 0.58-0.97; P = .03). Fewer clozapine-treated patients attempted suicide (34 vs 55; P = .03), required hospitalizations (82 vs 107; P =.05) or rescue interventions (118 vs 155; P = .01) to prevent suicide.10

Stopping clozapine was associated with increased risk, and there is signal that it may be helpful in other suicide risk groups:

No consensus exists as to whether other antipsychotic drugs share this effect. Discontinuation of clozapine is associated with increases in suicidality. Reductions in refractory suicidality/NSSI are observed in clozapine-treated patients with bipolar disorder or borderline personality disorder, but the evidence is limited.11

We have data that ketamine12, TMS13, and particularly SAINT-TMS14, and some psychedelic medicines15, including magnesium-ibogaine1617, can lead to rapid remission of depression, and it's concurrent suicidality, but we don't have a large-scale to prove that it prevents death by suicide.

The evidence is tantalizing enough to make this thread worth pulling:

Patients with SI demonstrated reduced ideation following TMS (F (1,21)=8.63, p <.01, ηp 2=.29; large effect), suggesting that depressive symptom change did not account for improvements in ideation.18

This is an independent effect from its effect on depression. This data is limited of course, because some of it isn't approved yet, and other forms of it are not paid for reliably enough to test the hypothesis. Most health plans exclude TMS for those with suicidal ideation, which is absolutely bonkers, to my mind. I would argue we all work to change that. Non-suicidal people are not the ones who complete suicide.

We offer such care at my company, Radial. Check us out.

Recommendation Five: Treasure Your Friendships

Friendships aren't just nice to have; they can help keep you alive. We have some data to back this up, particularly in rural settings:

After controlling for known risk factors for SI, low availability of social support at baseline was associated with greater likelihood of SI at 12-month follow-up.19

I've written about friendship before. Here are two quick guides to making and maintaining friends as an adult.

Also, sleep regularly…summarized here:

Recommendation Six: Please, Don’t Kill Yourself

I don't need a citation for this.

If you don't kill yourself, you're not gonna die. You're gonna have a chance to feel better, to feel less suicidal, to feel less alone, and your loved ones are not gonna be left, wondering what happened. Please, hang on, we love you, so much. We don't want to have to miss you. It might seem like it doesn't matter, but it really does. I don't care if you quit your job, I don't care if you leave everything behind, I don't care if you escape to Alaska. I do care if I never get to imagine seeing you ever again. Please, even if it feels like you can't stand it, you probably can. You're stronger than you know.

Don't let the soul sucking fuckers win. Here is a guided meditation to help. No, it's not one of those bullshit new age things. It's funny, try it out. And now, to reinforce your sense of self-sufficiency and feel slightly less alone, given this has been a problem for hundreds (and thousands) of years, I’ll close with the Bard:

MACBETH
How does your patient, doctor?


DOCTOR

Not so sick, my lord,
As she is troubled with thick-coming fancies
That keep her from her rest.


MACBETH

Cure ⌜her⌝ of that.
Canst thou not minister to a mind diseased,
Pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow,
Raze out the written troubles of the brain,
And with some sweet oblivious antidote
Cleanse the stuffed bosom of that perilous stuff
Which weighs upon the heart?

DOCTOR Therein the patient
Must minister to himself.

—Macbeth, Act 5, Scene 3

Share

Subscribe now

In loving memory, of all those who couldn't make it— may there be less of us to join you in the darkness till it’s due time, ever onward.

Find out how they think about the problem, and especially if they advertise working with suicidal people, or training in DBT, MBT, TFP, Schema Therapy, or the like, you won't be the first suicidal patient they've seen. You're unlikely to be the last.

The other benefit of this, from a practical standpoint, is that if you're having a really challenging day, and you have to talk to someone in your life about it, and they freak out, you can reassure that person by letting them know you're talking to your therapist about it. There's a tendency to chill out and assume that somebody has a handle on the problem, even if your jumpy, uncomfortable friend doesn't feel that way personally. Having a therapist is both practical and helpful.

Recommendation Three: Don’t Drink

Alcohol makes it endlessly more likely that you're gonna die by suicide. OK, that's hyperbole; it's not endlessly more likely; it's measurably and empirically more likely:

Prevalence estimates of alcohol abuse among completed suicides were mainly obtained in psychological autopsy studies and were reported in 8 reviews. The estimates varied between 15 and 61%.

And the authors further highlighted:

Prevalence of alcohol intoxication in completed suicide was covered by 3 reviews including altogether 35 adult population studies … prevalence rates ranged between 6 and 69 %.

Prevalence of alcohol intoxication in attempted suicide …was described in one review of 15 primary studies … and prevalence rates ranged between 10 and 73 %.

And certainly consider not being an alcoholic, or getting treatment for your alcohol use disorder, or maybe even just being a little bit quicker to get the GLP-1, as I wrote the other day :

Life time risk of suicide in alcohol abusers (i.e. alcoholics) was reviewed in one study (Murphy and Wetzel 1990) … ranging between 1.8 % and 6.2 %. 7

Recommendation Four: Don’t Use Coke or Other Drugs.

Similar to alcohol use disorder, cocaine use puts humans at higher rates of death by suicide, and if you're gonna abstain from any drug, if you're worried about suicide, it should be cocaine.

However, there are some individuals for whom this is particularly true. In that spirit of fully informed advice, I'm gonna highlight the individuals who are most likely to have a suicide attempt related to their cocaine use, because it's not equally risky for everybody.

Do you have childhood trauma? Then cocaine makes suicide attempts more likely:

The cocaine-dependent patients who had attempted suicide had significantly higher childhood trauma scores for emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse, emotional neglect, and physical neglect than the cocaine-dependent patients who had never attempted suicide…

And a family history of suicide makes cocaine a riskier choice:

Twenty-one of the 84 patients who had attempted suicide (25.0%) had a family history of suicidal behavior, compared with seven of the 130 patients who had never attempted suicide (5.4%) (χ2=15.58, df=1, p<0.0001; odds ratio=5.88, 95% CI=2.38–14.44).

It's not like people are doing thorough risk assessments before deciding to blow a line, but if you're unlike me and cool enough to be at parties where people might offer you cocaine, and you know that there's a risk of this, given your family history or personal history, you can now take that into account.

Unfortunately, other “fun” drugs of abuse are not known to be particularly safer, specifically opioids and cannabis:

Furthermore, one study found that opiates were present in 20% of suicide deaths, marijuana in 10.2%, cocaine in 4.6%, and amphetamines in 3.4% ( 2 ). Among the reported substances, alcohol and opioids are associated with the greatest risks of suicidal behavior. 8

Recommendation Five: Treat Your Psychiatric Illness, if You Have One

Psychiatric disorders, in Western cultures, are highly correlated with death by suicide. They're also highly prevalent, so it's not the most useful statistic in the world. That hasn't been said, there's some specific psychiatric disorders that are more likely to lead to your death than others, and if you know you have one of these, getting treatment is a priority if you either want to live, or really want to not die by suicide. I know those two things are not necessarily always the same, which is why I said it that way:

Ninety percent of people who die by suicide have one or more concomitant psychiatric disorders ( 3 ). Suicide risk is highest among patients with bipolar disorder (odds ratio=7.77) and unipolar affective disorder (odds ratio=6.67), followed by schizophrenia (odds ratio=6.55) and anxiety disorders (odds ratio=3.57–6.64). 9

If you have bipolar disorder, the answer is relatively easy, at least when it comes to the data, which is to give lithium a try. I've written about this extensively , but lithium-treated patients with bipolar disorder—who are axiomatically bipolar patients who can tolerate lithium—have an up to 800% reduction in the risk of death by suicide.

It works better if you take it, by the way:

The observed rates of suicide were 0.143, and of attempts, 2.01%/year, with a 5.2-fold (95% CI: 1.5–18.6) greater risk among patients consistently rated poorly versus highly adherent to lithium prophylaxis (11.4/2.2 acts/100 person-years).

Similarly, with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder, we have great data on clozapine in preventing suicide, even compared to an active treatment like olanzapine :

Suicidal behavior was significantly less in patients treated with clozapine vs olanzapine (hazard ratio, 0.76; 95% confidence interval, 0.58-0.97; P = .03). Fewer clozapine-treated patients attempted suicide (34 vs 55; P = .03), required hospitalizations (82 vs 107; P =.05) or rescue interventions (118 vs 155; P = .01) to prevent suicide. 10

Stopping clozapine was associated with increased risk, and there is signal that it may be helpful in other suicide risk groups:

No consensus exists as to whether other antipsychotic drugs share this effect. Discontinuation of clozapine is associated with increases in suicidality. Reductions in refractory suicidality/NSSI are observed in clozapine-treated patients with bipolar disorder or borderline personality disorder, but the evidence is limited. 11

We have data that ketamine 12 , TMS 13 , and particularly SAINT-TMS 14 , and some psychedelic medicines 15 , including magnesium-ibogaine 16 17 , can lead to rapid remission of depression, and it's concurrent suicidality, but we don't have a large-scale to prove that it prevents death by suicide.

The evidence is tantalizing enough to make this thread worth pulling:

Patients with SI demonstrated reduced ideation following TMS (F (1,21)=8.63, p <.01, ηp 2=.29; large effect), suggesting that depressive symptom change did not account for improvements in ideation. 18

This is an independent effect from its effect on depression. This data is limited of course, because some of it isn't approved yet, and other forms of it are not paid for reliably enough to test the hypothesis. Most health plans exclude TMS for those with suicidal ideation, which is absolutely bonkers, to my mind. I would argue we all work to change that. Non-suicidal people are not the ones who complete suicide.

Recommendation Five: Treasure Your Friendships

Friendships aren't just nice to have; they can help keep you alive. We have some data to back this up, particularly in rural settings:

After controlling for known risk factors for SI, low availability of social support at baseline was associated with greater likelihood of SI at 12-month follow-up. 19

Recommendation Six: Please, Don’t Kill Yourself

I don't need a citation for this.

If you don't kill yourself, you're not gonna die. You're gonna have a chance to feel better, to feel less suicidal, to feel less alone, and your loved ones are not gonna be left, wondering what happened. Please, hang on, we love you, so much. We don't want to have to miss you. It might seem like it doesn't matter, but it really does. I don't care if you quit your job, I don't care if you leave everything behind, I don't care if you escape to Alaska. I do care if I never get to imagine seeing you ever again. Please, even if it feels like you can't stand it, you probably can. You're stronger than you know.

Don't let the soul sucking fuckers win. Here is a guided meditation to help. No, it's not one of those bullshit new age things. It's funny, try it out. As she is troubled with thick-coming fancies

MACBETH

Cure ⌜her⌝ of that.
